notes: Adversarial suite of five synthetic matters, each planting one trap from the SKILL.md trap map (Where Mistakes Hide) in the requester's own premise, so a skill that follows the requester fails. Rows targeted: FMV valuation report and need (eval 1, Pennsylvania duplicative co-directorship with CFO retention email), compensation formula and amendments with the executed-agreement clocks (eval 2, Ohio retroactive increase and the 90-day writing rule), licensure of referral sources (eval 3, Florida nurse practitioner and per-patient marketer, party and scope), ownership charts and chain of contracts (eval 4, Ohio physician-owned PC per-click lease, stand in the shoes), and advisory opinions (eval 5, Illinois reliance on another system's OIG opinion). Every circuit rule in a Must line was read in full text for that forum: Greber for the Third Circuit (eval 1) and Borrasi for the Seventh (eval 5); evals 2 to 4 have no Must that depends on a circuit intent or causation rule. State law in a Must line is limited to Fla. Stat. 817.505, read in full. Labels are the exact labels in references/output-template.md. Key figures recomputed with a script: eval 2, the 90 consecutive days following Wednesday, July 1, 2026 end Tuesday, September 29, 2026; excess payments 3 x $2,000 = $6,000; October 30, 2026 is 121 days after July 1; eval 1, Dr. Shah's capped annual maximum is $21,600 (15 x $120 x 12) and her logged average is $12,960 a year against the proposed $150,000 fixed Kessler stipend. Every prompt supplies compensation terms, so the no-terms hard stop does not fire; none asks to backdate or for a fixed conclusion, and none involves dual representation. All parties are fictional. Today's date in every prompt is Friday, October 30, 2026.

evals.name: fmv-appraisal-offered-as-commercial-reasonableness
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are outside regulatory counsel to Keystone Valley Medical Center, an acute care hospital in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Keystone already has a signed medical director agreement with cardiologist Dr. Anita Shah (term January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2027) at $120 per documented hour, capped at 15 hours a month, for cardiovascular quality oversight, protocol development, cardiac catheterization lab oversight and peer review; her time logs average 9 hours a month. Keystone now proposes a written, two-year 'Co-Medical Director, Cardiovascular Services' agreement with interventional cardiologist Dr. Martin Kessler starting January 1, 2027, at a fixed $150,000 a year paid monthly, with no time-record requirement. His listed duties are quality oversight, protocol development, cath lab oversight and peer review. Dr. Kessler admits and refers Medicare patients to Keystone for inpatient and outpatient cardiac procedures. Summit Valuation's report concludes that $150,000 falls between the 50th and 75th percentiles of annual stipends for cardiology medical directorships and states: 'This report does not address commercial reasonableness.' In an email to the CEO, Keystone's CFO wrote: 'Kessler moved about 40% of his PCI cases to Mercy General last year. This directorship keeps him here.' The CEO's view is that the independent appraisal supports fair market value, so the arrangement is compliant. Please prepare the Stark and Anti-Kickback compliance analysis for the board and, if you agree with the CEO, a clean opinion letter.
evals.expected_output: Treats fair market value, commercial reasonableness and volume or value as separate tests, finds the appraisal silent on commercial reasonableness and the Kessler directorship duplicative of services already bought from Dr. Shah, labels it 'Stark: exception not met' as structured under the personal services and FMV compensation exceptions, treats the CFO email as referral-purpose evidence under the Third Circuit's one-purpose test (Greber), assigns 'AKS: no safe harbor; risk elevated', notes that the FMV exception's own AKS condition (411.357(l)(5)) fails with it, and declines to issue a clean opinion letter; hard stops checked and not triggered: compensation terms are supplied, no backdating is requested, the request asks for analysis rather than a conclusion regardless of it, and no dual representation is involved.
expected_behavior: Must: confirm the Stark threshold facts (Dr. Kessler is a physician, he refers Medicare patients for inpatient and outpatient hospital services, which are DHS, and the directorship is a direct compensation arrangement) before testing exceptions.
Must: state that fair market value, commercial reasonableness, and the volume or value standard are separate requirements, citing the CMS statement at 85 FR 77530.
Must: state that the Summit Valuation report does not establish commercial reasonableness because it expressly excludes that question.

Must: identify that the Kessler duties duplicate the duties Keystone already buys from Dr. Shah, whose logged hours are below her cap, and explain that duplicate arrangements for the same services are questionable under CMS guidance and may fail the reasonable-and-necessary element of 411.357(d)(1)(iii).
Must: identify the CFO email as evidence that one purpose of the payment is to retain Dr. Kessler's referrals and apply the one-purpose test of United States v. Greber (3d Cir.).

Must: explain that the FMV compensation exception at 411.357(l) requires that the arrangement not violate the AKS (411.357(l)(5)) and be commercially reasonable even if no referrals were made (411.357(l)(4)).
Must: assign the label 'Stark: exception not met' to the proposed arrangement as structured.
Must: assign the label 'AKS: no safe harbor; risk elevated'.
Must: recommend specific changes or alternatives, such as documenting a distinct need with distinct duties and time records, or not entering the arrangement.
Must not: issue an opinion letter concluding that the arrangement complies with the Stark Law or the AKS.
Must not: treat the appraisal's fair market value conclusion as sufficient for compliance.
evals.trap_note: Row: FMV valuation report, statement of need, existing contracts for the same services (with the AKS intent row). A weak skill accepts the CEO's premise that an FMV appraisal settles compliance and writes the clean letter. The trap is live because the appraisal expressly disclaims commercial reasonableness, the duties are identical to those of an existing director who is under her hour cap, and the CFO email shows a referral-retention purpose in the Third Circuit, where Greber's one-purpose test was read in full; the FMV exception's (l)(5) AKS condition ties the two analyses together.

evals.name: retroactive-rate-increase-and-90-day-signature-rule
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are counsel to Maumee River Hospital in Toledo, Ohio. Orthopedic surgeon Dr. Carlos Medina serves as medical director of the hospital's orthopedic service line under a written, signed two-year agreement that ran from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026 at a fixed $9,000 per month, which met the personal services exception when it expired. Dr. Medina performs surgery at the hospital and refers Medicare patients there for inpatient and outpatient surgery and imaging. Nobody renewed the agreement, and he kept performing the same duties after June 30. On Thursday, August 20, 2026, the hospital's VP of physician services agreed by phone to Dr. Medina's request to raise the fee to $11,000 per month 'effective July 1' because of a new joint-replacement program. The first document that shows the $11,000 rate is an accounts-payable voucher dated Monday, August 24, 2026. The hospital paid $11,000 for his July, August and September services on August 25, September 25 and October 23, 2026. Compliance discovered all of this on Monday, October 26, 2026. Nothing in the file suggests the increase was tied to his referrals. The VP's position is: 'Stark gives us 90 days to get signatures, so we can sign a renewal now at $11,000 effective July 1 and we are covered.' Please analyze our Stark and Anti-Kickback position and tell us what to do.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the $9,000 holdover after June 30 could qualify under 411.357(d)(1)(vii) only on the same terms, that the $11,000 rate is a modification that was not set in advance (decided August 20 for services from July 1 and first written August 24), that 411.354(d)(1)(ii)(C) makes the 90-day writing and signature rule unavailable for a modification, and that even measured from July 1 that 90-day period ended Tuesday, September 29, 2026; labels the period from July 1 'Stark: exception not met', analyzes the AKS separately, explains the 60-day overpayment rule and that Stark-only conduct goes to the CMS SRDP, and declines to treat a renewal signed now as a cure; hard stops checked and not triggered: compensation terms and dates are supplied, signing now with a stated retroactive effective date is not itself a backdating request, no fixed conclusion is demanded, and no dual representation is involved.
expected_behavior: Must: state that a holdover after the June 30, 2026 expiration satisfies 411.357(d)(1)(vii) only on the same terms and conditions as the expired agreement.

Must: conclude that the $11,000 rate was not set in advance for services furnished from July 1, 2026 through at least August 24, 2026, because it was decided on August 20 and first written on August 24.
Must: explain that 411.354(d)(1)(ii)(C) provides that the 90-day writing and signature rule in 411.354(e)(4) does not apply to a compensation modification.
Must: state that even on the VP's theory, the 90 consecutive calendar days following July 1, 2026 ended on September 29, 2026.
Must: assign the label 'Stark: exception not met' to the arrangement for the period beginning July 1, 2026.
Must: identify the $2,000 monthly excess over the holdover rate, totaling $6,000 for July through September, as payments that differ from the terms the holdover could protect.
Must: analyze the AKS separately and assign one AKS label from the skill's vocabulary.

Must: explain that the 60-day report-and-return deadline runs from identification of the overpayment and may be suspended during a timely good-faith investigation for up to 180 days or while an acknowledged SRDP or OIG SDP submission is pending.
Must: state that if counsel concludes the conduct raises only Stark liability, the disclosure route is the CMS SRDP and not the OIG SDP.
Must: recommend a prospective written amendment signed before the services it covers rather than a retroactive one.
Must not: state that signing a renewal now at $11,000 effective July 1, 2026 cures the July through October noncompliance.
evals.trap_note: Row: Compensation formula, amendments, rate-change emails (with the executed agreement and clocks row). A weak skill accepts the VP's reading that the 90-day signature rule covers the renewal and blesses a retroactive paper fix. The trap is live because 411.354(d)(1)(ii)(C) expressly excludes (e)(4) for modifications, the increase was decided after the July services began and first written on August 24, and the holdover protects only the $9,000 terms. Recomputed with a script: September 29, 2026 is 90 days after July 1 (a Tuesday); excess is 3 x $2,000 = $6,000; October 30 is 121 days after July 1.

evals.name: nurse-practitioner-and-marketer-outside-stark
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We represent Suncoast Home Health LLC, a Medicare-certified home health agency in Tampa, Florida, owned by two non-physician investors. Its 2025 admissions were 65% Medicare, 15% Medicaid managed care and 20% commercial. Two arrangements are in question. First, Rachel Ortiz, an unlicensed 'community liaison' engaged as a 1099 independent contractor, calls on physician and nurse practitioner offices and is paid $1,500 a month plus $200 for each patient Suncoast admits from an office she covers. Second, Dana Whitfield, APRN, a nurse practitioner at an independent primary care clinic who orders home health for her patients, has a written 'clinical advisory' agreement with Suncoast at $2,500 a month with no time records or deliverables; it began the month after she started referring patients to Suncoast, and she referred 46 patients in 2025. Neither Ortiz nor Whitfield has any ownership interest in Suncoast. Our outside consultant says Stark covers only physicians, so neither arrangement is a problem. Please confirm with a Stark analysis memo.
evals.expected_output: Labels both relationships 'Stark: not implicated' because neither referral source is a physician, then analyzes both under the AKS (per-patient payments to an independent contractor fall outside the employee and personal services safe harbors; the advisory fee lacks time records and began with referrals) and under the Florida Patient Brokering Act, whose prohibition is not limited to federal program patients (with its (3)(a) AKS-keyed exclusion addressed), assigns 'AKS: no safe harbor; risk elevated' to the Ortiz arrangement, and corrects the consultant's conclusion; hard stops checked and not triggered: compensation terms are supplied, no backdating or fixed conclusion is requested, and no dual representation is involved.
expected_behavior: Must: assign the label 'Stark: not implicated' to both arrangements because neither Ortiz nor Whitfield is a physician as defined in 42 U.S.C. 1395x(r), adopted at 42 C.F.R. 411.351.
Must: state that the AKS applies to any person who offers or pays remuneration to induce referrals of federal health care program business, regardless of whether the recipient is a physician.
Must: identify the $200 per admitted patient payment as compensation that varies with referrals and state that it does not meet the personal services safe harbor at 42 C.F.R. 1001.952(d)(1).
Must: state that the employee safe harbor (1001.952(i)) and the statutory employee exception are unavailable to Ortiz because she is an independent contractor.
Must: assign the label 'AKS: no safe harbor; risk elevated' to the Ortiz arrangement.
Must: identify the absence of time records or deliverables and the timing of the Whitfield agreement relative to her referrals as intent and fair market value risk factors under the AKS.
Must: analyze the Florida Patient Brokering Act, Fla. Stat. 817.505, stating that its prohibition applies to any person and is not limited to federal health care program patients.
Must: address the 817.505(3)(a) exclusion for payment practices not prohibited by the AKS.
Must: recommend restructuring or terminating the per-patient compensation and evaluating the look-back exposure.
Must not: conclude that the arrangements raise no legal issue because the Stark Law does not apply.
evals.trap_note: Row: Engagement letter, organization chart, licensure of each referral source (party and scope). A weak skill either runs a Stark exception analysis on non-physicians or, following the consultant, stops once Stark is ruled out. The trap is live because both referral sources are non-physicians, so Stark is genuinely not implicated, while 80% of admissions are federal program business, Ortiz is paid per admitted patient as a 1099 contractor, Whitfield's fee has no records and started with her referrals, and Florida's patient brokering statute (read in full) is not limited to federal program patients. No Must depends on the Eleventh Circuit's intent standard, which is [VERIFY]; per-patient payments are analyzed on their terms.

evals.name: physician-owned-practice-per-click-lease-stand-in-shoes
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are counsel to Lakeview Community Hospital in Toledo, Ohio. Ridgeline Cardiology Imaging PC is owned 50/50 by cardiologists Dr. Elena Park and Dr. Farid Haddad, who each receive half of its profits. Under a written three-year lease signed by the hospital and the PC on Monday, March 3, 2025, the PC leases a nuclear cardiology SPECT camera to the hospital two days a week at $425 per scan; an appraisal says $425 per scan is fair market value. About 60% of the scans are on patients referred by Dr. Park and Dr. Haddad, and the hospital bills Medicare for them as outpatient hospital services. The hospital's in-house memo concludes: 'The lease is with the PC, not the doctors, so there is no direct compensation arrangement. The per-unit rate is fair market value and does not vary with referrals, so under 411.354(c)(2)(ii) there is not even an indirect compensation arrangement. Stark is not implicated.' Please review the memo and give us your Stark and Anti-Kickback analysis.
evals.expected_output: Explains that because Dr. Park and Dr. Haddad own the PC (a physician organization) and their interests are not titular, each is deemed to stand in its shoes under 411.354(c)(1)(ii), making the lease a direct compensation arrangement so the indirect definition is never reached; tests the equipment rental and FMV exceptions and finds the per-unit charges for scans on patients referred by the lessor barred (411.357(b)(4)(ii)(B), (l)(3)(ii)), labeling it 'Stark: exception not met'; finds the equipment rental safe harbor unavailable because aggregate rental is not set in advance; hard stops checked and not triggered: compensation terms are supplied, no backdating or fixed conclusion is requested, and no dual representation is involved.
expected_behavior: Must: state that Dr. Park and Dr. Haddad, as owners of the PC, are deemed to stand in its shoes under 42 C.F.R. 411.354(c)(1)(ii) and therefore have a direct compensation arrangement with the hospital.
Must: state that the ownership interests are not titular because each physician receives half of the profits (411.354(c)(3)(ii)(C)).
Must: explain that because the arrangement is direct, the indirect compensation definition at 411.354(c)(2) and the exception at 411.357(p) do not decide the question.

Must: explain that under 411.354(c)(3)(i) referrals by the physicians count as referrals by the PC when applying the exception, so scans on their patients are services to patients referred by the lessor.

Must: state that the equipment rental exception bars per-unit rental charges to the extent they reflect services to patients referred by the lessor to the lessee (411.357(b)(4)(ii)(B)), and that the FMV compensation exception contains the same bar (411.357(l)(3)(ii)).
Must: assign the label 'Stark: exception not met'.

Must: state that the AKS equipment rental safe harbor at 1001.952(c) requires the aggregate rental charge to be set in advance, which a per-scan rate does not satisfy, and analyze the AKS risk separately.
Must: recommend restructuring the lease prospectively (for example, a fixed periodic rent set in advance) and a look-back of claims for scans on patients the two physicians referred.
Must not: adopt the in-house memo's conclusion that Stark is not implicated.
evals.trap_note: Row: Ownership charts, operating agreements, chain of contracts. A weak skill follows the memo into the indirect compensation definition and concludes that FMV per-unit pay means no financial relationship. The trap is live because the two referring cardiologists own the contracting PC with full profit rights, which triggers mandatory stand in the shoes, converting the lease into a direct arrangement where the per-click ban for lessor-referred patients applies to the 60% of scans they refer.

evals.name: oig-advisory-opinion-issued-to-another-hospital
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We are counsel to Prairie State Medical Center in Peoria, Illinois. It proposes a three-year cardiac catheterization lab co-management agreement with Heartland Cardiology Group LLC, which is owned by six interventional cardiologists who perform procedures at Prairie State and refer Medicare and Medicaid patients there. Proposed compensation: a fixed base fee of $300,000 a year; a quality incentive of up to $200,000 a year tied to door-to-balloon time, readmission and patient-safety metrics; and a 'growth component' of $150 for each cath lab procedure performed at Prairie State above 1,800 procedures a year. Prairie State's VP of strategy writes: 'OIG issued a favorable advisory opinion in 2023 to a health system in another state for a cath lab co-management arrangement with a base fee and a quality incentive. Ours copies its structure, so we are protected. Please give us the compliance opinion and a term sheet.' No valuation has been done yet.
evals.expected_output: Explains that an OIG advisory opinion binds only the Secretary and the requesting parties and no one else may rely on it (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7d(b)(4)(A); 42 C.F.R. 1008.53), that OIG opinions do not decide Stark questions and may not address fair market value (1320a-7d(b)(3)), identifies the per-procedure growth component as a material difference that the other opinion did not cover, analyzes it under the AKS one-purpose test of the Seventh Circuit (Borrasi) and the Stark volume or value standard (411.354(d)(5)), flags the missing valuation as a Critical item, and recommends removing the growth component and obtaining a valuation, with the option of the hospital's own advisory opinion requests; hard stops checked and not triggered: compensation terms are supplied, no backdating or fixed conclusion is requested, and no dual representation is involved.
expected_behavior: Must: state that an OIG advisory opinion is binding only as to the Secretary and the parties that requested it and that no other person may rely on it, citing 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7d(b)(4)(A) or 42 C.F.R. 1008.53.
Must: state that an OIG advisory opinion does not decide whether an arrangement complies with the Stark Law, and that Stark advisory opinions are issued by CMS under 42 U.S.C. 1395nn(g)(6).
Must: state that OIG advisory opinions may not address whether compensation is fair market value (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7d(b)(3)) and that Prairie State therefore needs its own valuation.
Must: identify the $150 per-procedure growth component as a material difference from the arrangement described in the other system's opinion.

Must: analyze the growth component under the Stark volume or value standard, explaining under 411.354(d)(5) that a formula including the physicians' referrals as a variable with a positive correlation takes them into account.
Must: analyze the growth component under the AKS using the Seventh Circuit's one-purpose test from United States v. Borrasi.
Must: list the missing valuation as a Critical open item and assign the opinion status 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must: recommend removing or redesigning the growth component and note the option of requesting the hospital's own OIG and CMS advisory opinions.
Must not: state that Prairie State is protected by the advisory opinion issued to the other health system.
Must not: draft a term sheet that includes the per-procedure growth component without flagging it as a compliance risk.
evals.trap_note: Row: OIG or CMS advisory opinions, prior counsel opinions (reliance). A weak skill accepts that copying another system's favorable OIG opinion confers protection and drafts the term sheet. The trap is live because 1008.53 bars reliance by non-requestors, the client added a per-procedure growth payment the other opinion never approved, OIG opinions cannot address Stark or FMV and no valuation exists, and Illinois sits in the Seventh Circuit, where Borrasi (read in full) adopts the one-purpose test.
